questions.stem: Approximately what percentage of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next?

options.text: 100% — all energy is transferred
About 50%
About 90%
About 10%

questions.explanation: Only about 10% of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next. The rest is lost through respiration (heat), egestion (faeces), and excretion (urine). This is why food chains rarely have more than 4-5 trophic levels — there is not enough energy to support more.

questions.stem: Why can a pyramid of numbers sometimes be inverted, but a pyramid of biomass rarely is?

options.text: Because pyramids of numbers are always inverted
Because biomass cannot be measured
Because biomass is always the same at every level
Because one large organism (like a tree) can support many smaller organisms, giving an inverted number pyramid, but its biomass still exceeds that of its consumers

questions.explanation: A pyramid of numbers can be inverted when one large producer (e.g., an oak tree) supports many small primary consumers (e.g., insects). However, the tree's biomass is much greater than the total biomass of the insects, so the pyramid of biomass is still upright. Pyramids of biomass are rarely inverted.

questions.stem: In the carbon cycle, how is carbon returned to the atmosphere?

options.text: Carbon is never returned to the atmosphere
Through respiration by all living organisms, combustion of fossil fuels, and decomposition
Only through photosynthesis
Only through combustion of fossil fuels

questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is returned to the atmosphere by: respiration (all living organisms release CO₂), combustion of fossil fuels and wood, and decomposition (decomposers respire as they break down dead organic matter). Photosynthesis removes CO₂ from the atmosphere.

questions.stem: What is the role of decomposers in an ecosystem?

options.text: They are primary consumers in food chains
They break down dead organic matter and waste, recycling nutrients back into the soil for plants to absorb
They produce oxygen through photosynthesis
They only eat dead animals

questions.explanation: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down dead organisms and waste products, releasing nutrients (minerals like nitrates and phosphates) back into the soil. This nutrient recycling is essential for ecosystem functioning — without decomposers, nutrients would remain locked in dead matter and would not be available for plant growth.

options.text: The conversion of nitrates into nitrogen gas
The release of nitrogen into the atmosphere by plants
The conversion of atmospheric nitrogen gas (N₂) into ammonia or nitrates that plants can use
The absorption of nitrogen by plant leaves

questions.explanation: Nitrogen fixation is the conversion of atmospheric nitrogen gas (N₂) into ammonia (NH₃) or ammonium ions (NH₄⁺) that can be used by plants. This is carried out by nitrogen-fixing bacteria (e.g., Rhizobium in root nodules of legumes) and by lightning. Plants cannot use N₂ directly.

questions.stem: What is the difference between abiotic and biotic factors?

options.text: Abiotic factors only affect plants; biotic factors only affect animals
Abiotic factors are non-living (temperature, light, water); biotic factors are living (predation, competition, disease)
They are the same thing
Abiotic factors are living; biotic factors are non-living

questions.explanation: Abiotic factors are non-living conditions that affect organisms: temperature, light intensity, water availability, soil pH, wind speed, CO₂ concentration. Biotic factors are living influences: predation, competition (interspecific and intraspecific), disease, and food availability.

questions.stem: How do you estimate the population of a species in a habitat using quadrats?

options.text: Place quadrats randomly, count organisms in each, calculate the mean per quadrat, then scale up to the total area
Place one quadrat in the area with the most organisms
Use a transect line and count organisms along it only
Count every individual in the entire habitat

questions.explanation: To estimate population: (1) place quadrats randomly across the habitat, (2) count the number of organisms in each quadrat, (3) calculate the mean number per quadrat, (4) calculate population = mean per quadrat × (total area ÷ quadrat area). Random placement and sufficient sample size are important for reliability.

questions.stem: What does a food chain show?

options.text: The transfer of energy from one organism to the next, starting with a producer
How organisms reproduce
Only which animals eat which other animals
The movement of water through an ecosystem

questions.explanation: A food chain shows the transfer of energy from one trophic level to the next, always starting with a producer (an organism that makes its own food, usually through photosynthesis). The arrows show the direction of energy flow: producer → primary consumer → secondary consumer → tertiary consumer.

questions.stem: How does deforestation affect the carbon cycle?

options.text: It only affects the nitrogen cycle, not the carbon cycle
It has no effect on the carbon cycle
It decreases atmospheric CO₂
It increases atmospheric CO₂ because fewer trees absorb CO₂ for photosynthesis, and burning/decomposing trees releases stored carbon

questions.explanation: Deforestation increases atmospheric CO₂ in two ways: (1) fewer trees means less CO₂ is removed from the atmosphere by photosynthesis, and (2) burning or decomposing the removed trees releases the carbon they stored back into the atmosphere as CO₂. This contributes to the enhanced greenhouse effect and climate change.

options.text: The variety of different species in a habitat, along with genetic variation within species and variation between ecosystems
The total number of organisms in a habitat
The size of the largest population in an ecosystem
The number of food chains in an ecosystem

questions.explanation: Biodiversity refers to the variety of life at multiple levels: species diversity (number of different species and their relative abundance), genetic diversity (variation in alleles within a species), and ecosystem diversity (variety of different habitats). Higher biodiversity generally means a more stable and resilient ecosystem.
